title: The Buffalo Bull Who Sits Down: the Grand River, the Greasy Grass, and the Grandmother's Country
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Grand River and the Name

stops.name: Grand River, the birth of the boy they call Slow
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the year is given as 1831 by most accounts and as late as 1837 by others, no register was kept, and month and day are unknown and defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: On the Grand River, in the country that will be called South Dakota, a Hunkpapa woman bears a son. No register is kept. The men who later write his life were not present, and they set the year down anywhere from 1831 to 1837. They name the boy Hunkesni, Slow, for the deliberation with which he does everything, and Hoka Psice, Jumping Badger. Slow does not mean dull. He grows up among people who read a horse or a stranger's face with the same unhurried care, and who take a decision made in haste for no decision at all.
suggested_refs: The Grand River country of the Hunkpapa, above the Missouri

stops.name: The Yellowstone above Miles City, the birthplace his family keeps
stops.date_confidence: traditional and contested; the family account gives no year of its own, and the coordinate is an inference from the phrase 'south of present-day Miles City' rather than a figure any source states
stops.campa: A great-grandson, Ernie LaPointe, tells interviewers in 2007 that the birth happened elsewhere: along the Yellowstone River, south of the town that becomes Miles City, Montana. The family holds this by descent. The Grand River account holds by repetition in print. Neither can be checked against a record, because no record exists, and the two claims sit three hundred miles apart on the same map. Both sites stand marked. Resolving them would require a document that was never made, by people who had no reason to make it.
suggested_refs: Ernie LaPointe's family testimony on the birthplace, given in interview in 2007

stops.name: Lakota country, the coup counted at fourteen
stops.date_confidence: traditional; dated only by his approximate age, which is itself uncertain by up to six years, and anchored to the Grand River home country because no source gives a location for the raid
stops.campa: At about fourteen he rides out with his father and his uncle Four Horns against the Crow. He carries a coup stick, which is not a weapon. A Crow warrior turns to face the charge and is struck with the stick before he can bring his own weapon up, and mounted Lakota see it done. Counting coup requires witnesses; a killing does not. The boy comes back having been seen. The raid survives in the Hunkpapa accounts and nowhere else, and it is dated only by an age that is itself a guess.
suggested_refs: The coup stick as an instrument of witnessed honour among the Plains nations

stops.name: Grand River, the father gives away his own name
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the feast follows the raid immediately in the accounts but carries no independent date
stops.campa: His father holds a feast and gives his own name away. Nothing about the transfer is written down anywhere; the feast is the record of it. The boy becomes Thathanka Iyotake, Buffalo Bull Who Sits Down, a bull settled on its haunches and not to be moved. With the name come an eagle feather for the coup, a warrior's horse, and a shield of buffalo hide. The father takes a lesser name for himself. From this feast the man carries the name that the United States Army will spend the next forty-five years learning how to spell.
suggested_refs: The name-giving feast and the transfer of Thathanka Iyotake from father to son

stops.name: Killdeer Mountain, Sully's two thousand
stops.date_confidence: attested, 28 to 29 July 1864; the chronology lens gave only the year 1864 and a coordinate 14 km southeast of the battlefield, and the corrected figures are used here
stops.campa: Brigadier General Alfred Sully brings roughly 2,200 soldiers with artillery against a village of Lakota, Dakota, and Yanktonai at the foot of Killdeer Mountain. Sitting Bull is named among the defenders, with Gall and the Dakota leader Inkpaduta. The village has bows and a scattering of firearms and no answer at all to field guns. The people are driven off the mountain and the lodges are burned behind them. Sully files it as a victory. The campaign does not end, and within a week the fighting has moved west into the badlands.
suggested_refs: The Killdeer Mountain battlefield in Dunn County, North Dakota

stops.name: The badlands of the Little Missouri, three days of harassment
stops.date_confidence: attested, 7 to 9 August 1864; the pin is the Medora locality, and the fighting was in the badlands south and west of the present town rather than at it
stops.campa: Sully pushes his column west through broken country where a wagon train can be watched for a day from one ridge and struck at the single place it must pass. The Lakota harass the march for three days in August in what the Army records as the Battle of the Badlands, or of the Little Missouri. The geography lens carried this as tradition; it is a documented engagement and stands retagged as attested. Sitting Bull's band is among those doing the harassing, in country that fights on their side.
suggested_refs: The Little Missouri badlands west of present Medora, North Dakota

stops.name: Near Marmarth, the bullet through the hip
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1864; no day is given and 01 is the default. The coordinate corrects a lens figure that sat 6 km west, on the Montana line
stops.campa: He attacks a wagon train near the place that will be Marmarth, on the Little Missouri, and a soldier's bullet takes him through the left hip and out at the small of the back. The wound is judged not serious and he keeps the saddle. It is one of very few injuries attested to him by name and by place, in a war where most wounds went into no record at all. He is in his early thirties. The northern plains have been fighting for two years and will fight for twenty-six more.
suggested_refs: The Little Missouri crossing near present Marmarth, Slope County, North Dakota

stops.name: Fort Berthold, the Missouri posts under raid
stops.date_confidence: a span, roughly 1865 to 1868, opened here at its earliest year; the chronology lens dated the whole campaign to 1866, which is impossible, and no individual raid is dated in the sources
stops.campa: Through the years of Red Cloud's war on the Bozeman road, Sitting Bull leads and joins war parties against the Missouri River posts and the nations allied to them. The raiding runs from about 1865 to 1868 and makes his name a military one where it had been a spiritual one. Fort Berthold's own history records an 1862 burning by Sioux raiders and does not name him. The attribution rests on the article about the man and not on the article about the fort, a distinction stated here rather than letting one source stand for three.
suggested_refs: The original Fort Berthold site, submerged under Lake Sakakawea since the mid-1950s

stops.name: Fort Stevenson, a post that does not yet exist
stops.date_confidence: the fort is built in 1867 and abandoned in 1883, so 1867 is the earliest possible year for any raid on it; no attack by Sitting Bull is recorded in the fort's own history, and the month is unknown
stops.campa: Fort Stevenson goes up in 1867, some nine miles southwest of the place that becomes Garrison, and comes down in 1883. That one date breaks a common summary of these years, which puts raids on all three Missouri forts in 1866: he cannot have raided in 1866 a post that stands in 1867. The fort's own record notes no attack by him whatever. What is attested is a campaign of several years against a line of posts. Which fort, and in which season, the sources do not carry, and none is supplied here.
suggested_refs: The Fort Stevenson site southwest of Garrison, North Dakota

segments.name: The Treaty He Would Not Sign

stops.name: The Powder River camp, the Black Robe reaches him
stops.date_confidence: attested to 19 June 1868 by De Smet's own dating. The coordinate is the pool's own suggestion and sits well up the Powder, whereas the council is described as four miles above the river's mouth on the Yellowstone; the discrepancy is recorded and not silently corrected
stops.campa: Father Pierre-Jean De Smet, a Jesuit forty-nine days out of Saint Louis, rides into a camp of five hundred lodges and more, carrying the government's terms. Sitting Bull does not go to Fort Laramie and never will. The treaty comes to him. He receives the priest with courtesy and answers plainly what the war has cost and who provoked it, naming the massacre at Fort Lyon. De Smet writes the answer down that month. It is among the very few things Sitting Bull says that reach paper through a hand that heard him say it.
stops.quote: I hardly sustain myself beneath the weight of white men's blood that I have shed.
stops.quote_source: Recorded by Pierre-Jean De Smet after a council with Sitting Bull, 19 June 1868; printed in Robert M. Utley, The Lance and the Shield (Henry Holt, 1993), pp. 79-80. De Smet's own published letters could not be reached (archive.org returned 404 or rate-limited on repeated fetch), so the translation is not independently confirmed.
suggested_refs: The historical marker for the De Smet council above the mouth of the Powder River (hmdb.org m=253651)
sources: Utley, The Lance and the Shield (1993), pp. 79-80, via Wikiquote

stops.name: The same camp, the refusal to sell
stops.date_confidence: same council as the preceding stop; the quotation is not separately dated in any source and is placed with the De Smet visit of June 1868
stops.campa: To the priest carrying the paper he gives the sentence that will be quoted for a century and a half, and it concerns land rather than blood. He will not sell. The distinction he draws is not about price. Under the Fort Laramie framework, land becomes a thing conveyed by signature, and he is declining to be the kind of person who conveys it. Norman E. Matteoni prints the line at page 41 of Prairie Man. An earlier draft of this research gave that author's name wrongly as Vincent; the correction stands.
stops.quote: I wish all to know that I do not propose to sell any part of my country.
stops.quote_source: Sitting Bull to Pierre-Jean De Smet, 1868, as given in Norman E. Matteoni, Prairie Man: The Struggle between Sitting Bull and Indian Agent James McLaughlin (TwoDot, 2015), p. 41, via Wikipedia; corroborated at teachingamericanhistory.org
suggested_refs: Matteoni, Prairie Man (2015), p. 41

stops.name: Fort Rice, the treaty signed by another man
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2 July 1868. The coordinate corrects a lens figure labelled 'near present Bismarck'; Fort Rice stood some thirty miles south of Mandan, between the mouths of the Heart and Cannonball
stops.campa: On the second of July the northern bands' council meets at Fort Rice on the Missouri, and the Treaty of Fort Laramie is signed there for them. Sitting Bull is not present. What happens in his absence is where the sources part: the account of the fort says he sent a replacement to sign in his stead, and the account of the man says he refused the treaty outright. Those are two different acts, and they describe two different men. Both are in print. His opposition to the treaty is not in question; the mechanism is, and no choice is made between them.
suggested_refs: The Fort Rice council of 2 July 1868 and the northern bands' signatures

segments.name: The Sun Dances and the Greasy Grass

stops.name: Rosebud country, the Sun Dance with the Cheyenne Ice
stops.date_confidence: the year 1875 is attested and the month is unknown, defaulted to June. The location is not attested at all: no source places the 1875 camp, and this pin is borrowed from the separate 1876 gathering and should be read as unverified
stops.campa: Northern Cheyenne, Hunkpapa, Oglala, Sans Arc, and Minneconjou camp together for a Sun Dance, and Sitting Bull enters into alliance with the Cheyenne medicine man Ice. In the dance he receives what Robert Utley, drawing on the late testimony of One Bull and White Bull, renders as a revelation concerning enemies not yet identified. Ice's own recorded remark is that no one then knew who the enemy were, of what tribe. The war with the United States is a year off. Nobody at this dance is told that, and nobody here knows where the camp stood.
stops.quote: The Great Spirit has given our enemies to us. We are to destroy them. We do not know who they are. They may be soldiers.
stops.quote_source: Sitting Bull at the 1875 Sun Dance, as given in Robert M. Utley, The Lance and the Shield (1992), pp. 122-24, quoted in Wikipedia. Utley narrates ('Sitting Bull intoned') from Lakota oral testimony gathered decades later, not from a contemporaneous transcript.
suggested_refs: Utley, The Lance and the Shield (1992), pp. 122-24, on the 1875 alliance with Ice
sources: Utley, The Lance and the Shield (1992), via Wikipedia

stops.name: Deer Medicine Rocks on the Rosebud, the hundred cuts
stops.date_confidence: approximately 5 June 1876, about three weeks before the Little Bighorn. The chronology lens gave 1876-06-17, which is the date of the Battle of the Rosebud, a different event; the correction follows Wikipedia's Little Bighorn article
stops.campa: He dances against the sun with his back to a cottonwood pole while a relative cuts fifty pieces of skin from each arm, more than a hundred cuts, and the blood runs down to the wrists. He fasts and stares into the sun and falls, and when he can speak he describes soldiers dropping into the camp upside down, like grasshoppers, with their hats coming off. The bands take it exactly as told: the soldiers are given, and the dead must not be robbed afterward. Three weeks later the Seventh Cavalry comes down the Little Bighorn.
suggested_refs: Deer Medicine Rocks on Rosebud Creek, site of the June 1876 Sun Dance

stops.name: The Rosebud, a battle he may not have fought
stops.date_confidence: the battle date is firm; Sitting Bull's presence and role on the day are not established by any source consulted, and the stop is entered as an open gap rather than as an event in his own itinerary
stops.campa: Crazy Horse takes the warriors up the Rosebud against General Crook's column and fights him to a standstill, eight days after the Sun Dance and a week before the Little Bighorn. Where Sitting Bull is that day, the reachable sources do not settle. General accounts put him in camp with his arms still raw from the hundred cuts, present but not fighting. The encyclopedia article on the battle does not mention him at all. The gap is marked as a gap instead of being filled with the likelier of two guesses.
suggested_refs: The Rosebud battlefield, Big Horn County, Montana
sources: Wikipedia, 'Battle of the Rosebud' (no mention of Sitting Bull located)

stops.name: The Little Bighorn, the camp of ten thousand
stops.date_confidence: the camp is attested for mid to late June 1876; the day given here is the eve of the battle and the population figures are estimates that vary across accounts. The coordinate is the atlas's canonical Little Bighorn pin, inherited unchanged
stops.campa: Along the west bank of the Greasy Grass the allied camp runs for miles: about eighteen hundred lodges in six circles, the Hunkpapa at the southern end, and by mid-June more than ten thousand people drawn in from every band that will come. It is the largest gathering of Plains people anyone alive has seen, and it exists because Sitting Bull is in it. He holds no rank an army would recognise. What he holds is the reason the circles are pitched next to one another at all, and there is no office in it that an order can be served on.
suggested_refs: The village site along the Little Bighorn, called the Greasy Grass

stops.name: The Little Bighorn, Custer's column destroyed
stops.date_confidence: attested. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from the atlas's existing Little Bighorn pin, shared with the queued entries for Low Dog, Custer, and Reno
stops.campa: Custer's scouts find the camp and Custer attacks it with a divided regiment on a hot Sunday afternoon. Sitting Bull takes no fighting part: he is inside the camp, moving the women and children away from the river, while Crazy Horse and Gall lead the counterattack that rolls up the five companies on the ridge. Low Dog, elsewhere rendered Perro Bajo, fights in the same hour. In something under an hour the column ceases to exist, and the United States begins the war it believed it had already won.
suggested_refs: Last Stand Hill and the Hunkpapa circle at the southern end of the village

stops.name: Cedar Creek, the parley between the lines
stops.date_confidence: attested to 21 October 1876. The geography lens had flagged this engagement as unverifiable and pinned it near Terry, Montana; it is fully documented and the pin moves about 110 km northwest
stops.campa: Colonel Nelson Miles brings the Fifth Infantry against the Hunkpapa near Cedar Creek and Big Dry Creek and asks to talk. The two men meet on open ground between their own lines and talk twice. Miles wants the bands on a reservation and Sitting Bull wants the soldiers out of the buffalo country, and neither offer contains anything the other can take. The talks break down and the fighting starts the same day. Six days later more than four hundred lodges come in and surrender to Miles. Sitting Bull's own people are not among them.
suggested_refs: The Cedar Creek and Big Dry Creek ground, Montana Territory, October 1876

stops.name: The Milk River borderlands, the winter march north
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the sources carry this winter as summary narrative and fix no camp and no day between October 1876 and May 1877. The date and pin are a midpoint of the described movement, not an attested position
stops.campa: Miles keeps columns in the field through the cold, which no one had done to them before, and the band moves north across country with the buffalo thinning ahead of it. People die of cold and of hunger on the way. This whole winter comes down as summary rather than as dated engagements, carried here as reconstruction: the route, the losses, and the direction are agreed by every account, and not one of them fixes a camp or a day. Five months of a man's life, present in the record only as a vector.
suggested_refs: The Milk River and Frenchman's Creek country of northern Montana Territory
sources: Wikipedia, 'Sitting Bull' (general narrative of the flight north)

stops.name: The medicine line, crossing into Canada
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1877; no day is given and 01 is the default
stops.campa: In May he takes his people over the forty-ninth parallel into the North-West Territories of Queen Victoria, whom the Lakota call the Grandmother. The line is invisible and absolute: American cavalry cannot cross it, and everybody on both sides knows it. The far side is not safety. It is a shrinking buffalo range already shared with Blackfoot, Cree, and Metis who were there first, and the arithmetic of it is against him from the first week. The exile is meant to last until the hunting recovers. It lasts four years and ends in a surrender.
suggested_refs: The forty-ninth parallel, called the medicine line by the Lakota

stops.name: Pinto Horse Butte, the red coat rides in alone
stops.date_confidence: the meeting is attested to 1877, within weeks of the crossing, and the chronology lens's date of 1879 is wrong; the month is not given and June is a default. The pin is Wood Mountain Post, near which the Hunkpapa camp lay
stops.campa: Superintendent James Morrow Walsh of the North-West Mounted Police rides into the Hunkpapa camp with a handful of men and states the terms: obey Canadian law, do not raid across the line, and no one will hand you back. Walsh keeps his half of it, and Sitting Bull holds him to it for four years. The year matters, because the meeting is often printed as 1879. Walsh met him in 1877, weeks after the crossing, and not at the fort that carries his name. Fifty thousand square miles of prairie, and a police force of a few hundred men.
suggested_refs: Wood Mountain Post Provincial Park, Saskatchewan, and the camp near Pinto Horse Butte

stops.name: Fort Walsh, the American commissioners refused
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1877; the day is not established in the material consulted and 01 is the default. The coordinate corrects a lens figure sitting about 4 km south of the fort
stops.campa: The United States sends General Alfred Terry into Canada with a commission to offer terms, and the meeting is held at Fort Walsh in the Cypress Hills under Mounted Police guard. Sitting Bull refuses. He has been given a country here, he tells them, and does not propose to go back to men whose word has not held once. Terry goes home with nothing. This is the encounter most often confused with Walsh's ride into the camp, which happened in another year and another place. The Fort Walsh article mentions neither.
suggested_refs: Fort Walsh in the Cypress Hills, seat of the October 1877 Terry Commission meeting

stops.name: The Cypress Hills, tobacco with Crowfoot
stops.date_confidence: undated; the meeting falls somewhere within the exile of 1877 to 1881 and no source consulted narrows it. The date given is the midpoint of that span and carries no authority
stops.campa: Crowfoot leads the Blackfoot, who have fought the Lakota for as long as either nation remembers, and the two men are now hunting the same emptying country under the same police. They meet and exchange tobacco, which between them is a treaty. Sitting Bull thinks well enough of the man to give one of his own sons the name Crowfoot. No source consulted dates the meeting. It happens somewhere in four years, and the middle of them is where it is placed, without claiming the year to be exact.
suggested_refs: Crowfoot of the Siksika and the tobacco exchange of the exile years

stops.name: Fort Qu'Appelle, a place-name and nothing else
stops.date_confidence: no date exists. Secondary accounts mention Qu'Appelle in passing during the exile and attach no event, no year, and no month; the date shown is a placeholder within 1877 to 1881 and should not be read as a claim
stops.campa: Accounts of the Canadian years mention Qu'Appelle in passing, a mention recorded here rather than quietly dropped. What cannot be said is when he was there, why, or whether he was there at all. The encyclopedia article on the town does not name him. No dated event attaches. The pin sits on the town because a pin must sit somewhere, and the town is the only fixed thing in the claim. This is the weakest point on the map and is marked as such.
suggested_refs: Fort Qu'Appelle, Saskatchewan, named in passing in accounts of the exile
sources: General secondary references to the Canadian exile; not corroborated by the Wikipedia article on Fort Qu'Appelle, which does not mention him

stops.name: Fort Buford, the rifle handed over
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He comes back over the line with 186 people, most of them family, all of them hungry, and gives himself up at Fort Buford where the Yellowstone meets the Missouri. His son Crow Foot, a boy, carries the Winchester across to Major David Brotherton and lays it down, so that the father does not surrender it with his own hands. In the same years, on the far side of the hemisphere, Julio Argentino Roca is running the Conquista del Desierto against the nations of the pampas. Neither campaign has heard of the other.
stops.quote: I wish it to be remembered that I was the last man of my tribe to surrender my rifle.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Sitting Bull at the Fort Buford surrender, 19 July 1881, addressed to Major David H. Brotherton; widely repeated and quoted in Wikipedia citing PBS and Utley. The original 1881 dispatch and Brotherton's report could not be reached (PBS pages returned no matching text on fetch), so the wording is unverified by direct inspection.
suggested_refs: The Fort Buford surrender ground at the Yellowstone and Missouri confluence
working/journeys/julio_argentino_roca.journey.json, for the contemporaneous Conquista del Desierto

stops.name: Fort Buford, the question about his son
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the commanding officer's quarters, with soldiers and his own warriors listening, he says he wishes to regard the soldiers and the white race as friends, and then asks the question that has no answer in the room: who will teach his son the new ways of the world. The man who put the rifle into the boy's hands the day before is asking what the boy is now for. Crow Foot will be shot dead beside his father nine winters from this room, still a boy, and nobody will have answered.
suggested_refs: The Commanding Officer's Quarters at Fort Buford, preserved on the site

stops.name: Standing Rock Agency, counted in a book
stops.date_confidence: attested. The coordinate corrects a chronology figure used for three separate Standing Rock entries that sits about 17 km south of the agency
stops.campa: William T. Selwyn goes through the band with a census book and writes down twelve people in Sitting Bull's immediate family, and forty-one families, one hundred and ninety-five people, in the band entire. This is the administrative act the surrender was for. A people counted in lodges are now counted in households, on a printed form, at an agency, against rations that can be withheld. The agency stands at Fort Yates on the Missouri, and everything left of his life will happen within a day's ride of it.
suggested_refs: The Selwyn census of 26 August 1881 at Standing Rock Agency

stops.name: Fort Randall, twenty months a prisoner of war
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1881; no day is given and 01 is the default. The detention runs about twenty months, to May 1883
stops.campa: Instead of going to the agency he is put on a steamboat with a hundred and seventy-two followers and carried down the Missouri to Fort Randall, and held there as a prisoner of war for twenty months. Photographers come down to make portraits. Newspapermen come to ask about the Custer fight and he answers them; Low Dog and Gall have already given their versions to the press and he is replying to those as much as to the reporters. He is famous now, and he is inside a stockade, and the two facts arrive together.
stops.quote: There was a Great Spirit who guided and controlled that battle. I could do nothing.
stops.quote_source: Sitting Bull on the Custer fight, in W. Fletcher Johnson, Life of Sitting Bull and History of the Indian War of 1890-91 (1891), p. 154, introduced 'Speaking of the Custer fight, Sitting Bull said:'. Johnson is a hastily assembled popular compilation reprinting newspaper interviews; cite it as a period press account, not a verified transcript.
suggested_refs: The Fort Randall stockade near present Pickstown, South Dakota
D. F. Barry's Fort Randall and Standing Rock portraits of the early 1880s
sources: W. Fletcher Johnson, Life of Sitting Bull (1891), p. 154

stops.name: Standing Rock, the return and a baptism that may not have happened
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1883; no day is given. The baptism report is dated only to 1883 and is placed here for want of a narrower date
stops.campa: He comes back up the river in May to Standing Rock and to the supervision of the agent James McLaughlin, who will be the fixed opposing pressure of his last seven years. In the same period the New York Times reports that he has been baptised a Catholic. McLaughlin calls the report an error. Both statements survive and neither party produces a baptismal record. The claim stands as reported and disputed, because that is the condition it arrives in.
suggested_refs: Agent James McLaughlin's administration of Standing Rock, 1881 to 1895
sources: Wikipedia, 'Sitting Bull', citing contemporary New York Times reporting disputed by McLaughlin

stops.name: Bismarck, the speech at the railway ceremony
stops.date_confidence: genuinely contested. Popular retellings say September 1883 at Bismarck; Wikipedia says 1884, citing Edward Lazarus, Black Hills/White Justice (1991), p. 106. Neither is asserted here and the date printed is the earlier of the two
stops.campa: He is brought out to speak at a ceremony for the completed Northern Pacific Railway, and the story that follows him afterward is that he greeted the crowd in Lakota with insults while the Army interpreter recited a prepared courtesy and the audience applauded. Michael Hiltzik gives two separated fragments of it in Iron Empires, which retellings run together into one speech. Robert Utley says flatly that Sitting Bull did not curse his audiences. Even the year is contested. No Lakota text exists, and no quotation is printed here.
suggested_refs: Michael Hiltzik, Iron Empires (2020), p. 261, and Utley 1993, p. 263, for the two sides of the anecdote
sources: Hiltzik, Iron Empires (2020), p. 261, via Wikipedia
Lazarus, Black Hills/White Justice (1991), p. 106, via Wikipedia

segments.name: The Show Years and the Grand River House

stops.name: Saint Paul, Little Sure Shot
stops.date_confidence: the year 1884 is attested and the month and day are unknown, defaulted to 01-01. The Minnesota venue is attested; the Saint Paul pin is the standard locality anchor for it
stops.campa: On a tour got up by the promoter Alvaren Allen and billed as the Sitting Bull Connection, he watches a small woman from Ohio shoot at a Minnesota theatre and is impressed enough to seek her out afterward. Annie Oakley is twenty-four and shoots better than anyone he has seen do it. He adopts her as a daughter in the Lakota manner and gives her the name Watanya Cicilla, which the show bills render as Little Sure Shot. She keeps his photograph in her house for the rest of her life.
suggested_refs: The 'Sitting Bull Connection' tour of 1884 and Annie Oakley's adoption name, Watanya Cicilla

stops.name: Montreal, four months with Buffalo Bill
stops.date_confidence: the year and the four-month duration are attested; the month boundaries are not. Standard accounts have him joining in June and leaving in October, and the chronology lens's April to August framing is an unsourced narrowing and is dropped
stops.campa: He joins Buffalo Bill Cody's Wild West and rides once around the arena each performance for about fifty dollars a week, four months of it, selling his autograph and his photograph for whatever the crowd will pay. In Montreal the Notman studio sits him down beside Cody for the picture that outlives them both. He gives most of the money away to the ragged boys who follow him in every city. The show will cross to Paris in 1889 and play beneath the tower Gustave Eiffel is raising on the Champ de Mars; he is not with it, and never sees Europe.
stops.quote: The white man knows how to make everything, but he does not know how to distribute it.
stops.quote_source: Sitting Bull to Annie Oakley during the Buffalo Bill's Wild West tour, c. 1885, as recounted in Dee Brown, Bury My Heart at Wounded Knee (1970), reproduced in full on Wikiquote. Brown is a secondary synthesis and gives no primary footnote for the exchange.
suggested_refs: The Notman studio photograph 'Sitting Bull and Buffalo Bill, Montreal, Quebec, Canada, 1885'
working/journeys/gustave_eiffel.journey.json, for the 1889 Champ de Mars season he did not attend
sources: Dee Brown, Bury My Heart at Wounded Knee (1970), via Wikiquote

stops.name: Grand River, Caroline Weldon in the house
stops.date_confidence: the year 1889 is attested for her arrival; the month is not given and June is a default
stops.campa: Caroline Weldon comes out from Brooklyn with her young son Christie to the compound on the Grand River, a white woman of the National Indian Defense Association who will act as his secretary, his interpreter, and his advocate against further cessions of land. The agency and the newspapers treat the arrangement as a scandal and print it that way. She paints his portrait. She stays into the Ghost Dance winter and leaves before the end of it, and the land commissions get their signatures anyway, from other men.
suggested_refs: Caroline Weldon's painted portraits of Sitting Bull, made at the Grand River compound

stops.name: Standing Rock, the Ghost Dance comes east
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1890 for the movement's arrival at Standing Rock; no day is given
stops.campa: The dance comes east out of Nevada from the Paiute prophet Wovoka: dance, and the dead return, and the buffalo return, and the whites go away without a shot being fired. It reaches Standing Rock in the autumn and Sitting Bull lets the dancers gather at his camp on the Grand River. He does not appear to dance himself. What he does is decline to forbid it, and to the agency that is the same thing as leading it. The reports going up the line from McLaughlin's desk name him the instigator.
suggested_refs: Wovoka's Ghost Dance and its eastward spread from Nevada to the Dakota agencies

stops.name: Standing Rock Agency, the arrest order drafted
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: McLaughlin has wanted him removed for years and now has a reason he can put in writing: the fear that Sitting Bull will leave the reservation with the dancers. He drafts the instructions for the arrest on the fourteenth of December and gives the work to the Indian police, Lakota men in agency uniform, rather than to the Army, which is close by and waiting. The choice is deliberate. Whatever happens at the cabin on the Grand River will happen between Hunkpapa and Hunkpapa, and the paperwork will say so.
suggested_refs: McLaughlin's arrest instructions of 14 December 1890

stops.name: Grand River, thirty-nine police before dawn
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Before light, about thirty-nine Indian police and four volunteers under Lieutenant Bull Head ride down to the cabin. They come into the house, wake him, and tell him he is under arrest. He agrees to go and asks that his horse be saddled, the grey the Wild West gave him. Outside, his people are coming out of the other lodges and gathering around the police, and their number grows while the officers stand in the yard waiting for a man to finish dressing. Everyone in the yard knows every man in the doorway.
suggested_refs: Sitting Bull's cabin on the Grand River, Standing Rock Reservation

stops.name: Grand River, the shots at the door
stops.date_confidence: attested; the death is placed between twelve and one in the afternoon
stops.campa: Catch-the-Bear brings a rifle out of the crowd and shoots Lieutenant Bull Head, and Bull Head, falling, fires his revolver into Sitting Bull's chest. Red Tomahawk shoots him in the head. He dies between twelve and one in the afternoon. Eight policemen die, six on the spot and two later of wounds, and seven of his men besides himself, one of them his son Crow Foot. The grey show horse, trained to sit up at the sound of a gun, sits up in the middle of it; that part is told everywhere and written down nowhere at the time.
suggested_refs: The Grand River arrest site and the graves of the Indian police killed there

stops.name: Fort Yates, the coffin and the quicklime
stops.date_confidence: the transport and burial follow the killing immediately; the exact day of interment is not fixed in the sources and 17 December is the conventional figure
stops.campa: The body goes up to Fort Yates and an Army carpenter builds a coffin for it, and it is put into the post cemetery in an unmarked grave, with quicklime, without ceremony. The quicklime comes down through the descendants as grievance rather than through the Army as record. Fourteen days later the Seventh Cavalry, Custer's old regiment, kills some three hundred Lakota at Wounded Knee Creek. Within a month the Ghost Dance is finished as a movement in the Dakotas, and the grave at Fort Yates has no name on it.
stops.quote: What treaty that the whites have kept has the red man broken? Not one. What treaty that the whites ever made with us red men have they kept? Not one.
stops.quote_source: Sitting Bull as recalled by W. H. H. 'Adirondack' Murray in a memorial published in the New York World shortly after the killing, reprinted in W. Fletcher Johnson, Life of Sitting Bull (1891), pp. 195-203, the quoted passage at p. 201. A white memorialist's posthumous recollection, not a transcript; no occasion or date is given for the original utterance.
suggested_refs: The original Fort Yates post cemetery grave and its surviving marker
sources: W. Fletcher Johnson, Life of Sitting Bull (1891), p. 201

stops.name: Chicago, the cabin on show at the Exposition
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition; the month of the cabin's display is not given and May is the fair's opening month
stops.campa: The log cabin from the Grand River is taken apart, freighted to Chicago, and put back together on the grounds of the World's Columbian Exposition, where the public pays to look at the room in which he was shot. Ghost Dance survivors are still confined at Pine Ridge in the same season. Nothing about the exhibit is presented as the site of a killing; it is billed as an ethnographic curiosity, a relic of wars three years old. A nation that could not beat him in the field in 1876 charges admission to his front room in 1893.
suggested_refs: The Sitting Bull cabin exhibit at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, Chicago

stops.name: Mobridge, the grave under concrete
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1953; no day is given. The coordinate corrects a chronology figure sitting about 4.5 km northeast of the monument, in the river
stops.campa: In April a party of Lakota family members, backed by Mobridge businessmen who want the grave on their own side of the state line, opens the Fort Yates plot at night, takes what it finds, and reburies it on a bluff over the Missouri near his birth country. They pour concrete over it so that nobody can do to them what they have just done. Korczak Ziolkowski, who is carving Crazy Horse out of a mountain further west, cuts the granite bust that marks the spot. The site enters the National Register in 2006.
suggested_refs: The Sitting Bull Monument in Corson County, South Dakota, carved by Korczak Ziolkowski

stops.name: Fort Yates, the marker that does not move
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the dispute begins with the 1953 removal and continues, and the date shown marks the day after the exhumation rather than any single event
stops.campa: North Dakota does not accept the removal. A marker stays at the original grave in the post cemetery and the state goes on saying he is in it, while South Dakota says he is on the bluff at Mobridge. Whether the 1953 party took the right remains, or all of them, or any of them, is disputed: the exhumation was hasty, poorly documented, and followed by no examination of what came out of the ground. Two states claim one grave and both maintain a site. Neither claim is adjudicated here.
suggested_refs: The surviving marker at the original Fort Yates gravesite
sources: regional dispute reported in secondary accounts, not adjudicated

stops.name: Washington, the hair returned from the Smithsonian
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Ernie LaPointe, a great-grandson, takes back from the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History a lock of Sitting Bull's hair and a pair of his leggings, cut from the body in 1890 and kept in a drawer for a hundred and seventeen years. The return is made under the repatriation act, and LaPointe holds a private ceremony for the objects afterward. A sample of the hair survives that ceremony. It will be asked a question that nobody in 1890, and nobody in the museum, could have known to ask of it.
suggested_refs: The NAGPRA repatriation of 5 December 2007 from the National Museum of Natural History

stops.name: Standing Rock, the camps against the pipeline
stops.date_confidence: the camps run from spring 2016 into early 2017; August 2016 marks their growth to national scale, and the invocation of his name is reported throughout rather than on any single date
stops.campa: Thousands come to camps near the confluence of the Cannonball and the Missouri to stop a pipeline crossing upstream of the Standing Rock water intake, and Sitting Bull's name and face are carried there on banners and in speeches. The link asserted is direct: the man who would not sell his country, and the people who will not have a pipe run beneath their water. That framing is everywhere in the coverage of 2016 and 2017, and nothing here verifies it against a primary document.
suggested_refs: The Oceti Sakowin and Sacred Stone camps at the Cannonball confluence, 2016 to 2017
sources: widely reported contemporaneous framing in Standing Rock coverage, not independently verified

stops.name: Copenhagen, the answer taken out of the hair
stops.date_confidence: attested to 27 October 2021, the publication date of the paper
stops.campa: A team under Eske Willerslev, working with degraded autosomal DNA drawn from the hair sample, publishes a match confirming that Ernie LaPointe and his three sisters are Sitting Bull's biological great-grandchildren. It is reported as the first published use of the technique to establish descent from a named historical person across such a gap in time. The journal is Science Advances and not Science, an error that travels with almost every popular account of the finding. LaPointe's family has asked that the remains be moved again, to the Little Bighorn. They are still on the bluff at Mobridge.
suggested_refs: Moltke, Korneliussen, Seguin-Orlando, Moreno-Mayar, LaPointe, Billeck and Willerslev, 'Identifying a living great-grandson of the Lakota Sioux leader Tatanka Iyotake (Sitting Bull)', Science Advances 7(44), eabh2013
